Inimical

/ih-NIM-ih-kul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inimical means hostile, harmful, or unfavorable in nature or effect, especially when describing conditions or surroundings.

The thin, dry air of the high desert proved inimical to the ferns, which shriveled within days of being planted there.

Worked Example

A grower planted a row of young lemon trees a hundred yards from a windy shoreline. Salt spray coated the leaves at every high tide, and the sandy soil drained away every drop of fresh water within minutes. Nothing at the site was obviously poisonous, yet not one tree ever put out healthy growth. The conditions were simply inimical to citrus.

The site's conditions worked actively against the trees rather than merely failing to help them, which is what inimical describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

adverse: Adverse means working against success or wellbeing, and it is the mild, official-sounding word - adverse weather, adverse effects. Inimical is stronger and more pointed: the conditions behave almost like an enemy of whatever tries to live or work in them. An adverse season sets the orchard back; an inimical climate means the orchard should never have been planted.

hostile: Hostile means unfriendly and actively opposed, and it attaches naturally to people and their intentions - a hostile crowd, a hostile takeover. Inimical does the same work for impersonal things: climates, chemistries, and policies that harm without meaning to. A hostile guard wants you gone; an inimical desert has no wants at all, yet works against you just the same.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

favorable: helping something succeed or thrive

hospitable: offering conditions in which something can live comfortably

Where it sits · how damaging the conditions are — unhelpful → inimical → lethal

unhelpful vs. inimical: Unhelpful conditions merely fail to assist, while inimical conditions work against whatever is trying to survive in them.

lethal vs. inimical: Inimical conditions make survival difficult, but lethal ones kill outright.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in

Prefix — in: not

Root — imic

Root — imic: from Latin amicus, friend

Suffix — al

Suffix — al: characteristic of, pertaining to, having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Inimical comes from Latin inimicus, from in- ('not') plus amicus ('friend'), finished off with the suffix -al ('characteristic of, pertaining to'). Read the pieces in order and the word means 'characteristic of being un-friendly,' which is why conditions inimical to a crop behave like an enemy of it.

Use the root in a new word: amity

Use the root in a new word: amity: Two nations that sign a treaty of amity are pledging friendship, built on the very Latin amicus that inimical turns inside out.

Word Choice

formal, academic and scientific register

Inimical is nearly always followed by 'to' plus whatever is being harmed, as in 'inimical to plant growth' or 'inimical to open debate.' It usually describes conditions, climates, policies, or environments rather than a person's temperament; for an unfriendly person, plain 'hostile' is the better word.
